title: Dust Motes
narrative: A window cuts a wedge through a closed parlor. Specks drift, rise, fall.
Stillness that is still alive. The room has been shut; time is visible because the air has a population.
Use it when quiet should not be empty: a church, a bedroom, a barn in late sun. It is the wrong tool when the air is a ribbon from a cigarette ( Smoke ) or a soup that hides the far wall ( Fog ).
It is the wrong tool when the particles are on fire ( Sparks and Embers ). If the whole room is milky, you filled it.
Motes need a dark surround and a hard beam.
how: Create a shaft (window, slats, a cut HMI) and keep off-beam air darker. Introduce fine particles (real dust, atmosphere in small amounts).
Backlight or sidelight the beam; motes are seen by scatter toward camera. Slow movement: convection, not wind.
Prompt: dust motes hanging in a shaft of light around [Subject], slow particles, a room that has been closed, time made visible.
when: Use it for a pause, a prayer, a house that remembers. Do not use it in a gale or a nightclub wash.
If the camera is racing, motes become streaks or noise. Pair with Slow Motion only if you want to inventory the specks.
vs: Volumetric Light is the shaft; dust motes are the countable inhabitants of that shaft. Smoke is a continuous volume.
Sparks and Embers are incandescent and short-lived. Atmospheric Haze pales the far plane.
Motes are slow, discrete, and local to the beam.
examples_film: The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford lets window light populate air so interiors feel timed. The Tree of Life hangs specks in domestic and cosmic shafts.
Use beam plus specks, not a dusty grade on a flatly lit room.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Smoke fill or Volumetric Light with no specks. The tell: milky room, no shaft, or sparks.
The fix: a hard beam, dark off-beam, countable slow particles, backlight.

faq.q: What is Dust Motes in film?
faq.a: Dust motes are individual particles visible in a shaft of light. They make still air readable as matter and time, without turning the whole room into fog.

faq.q: Dust Motes vs Volumetric Light
faq.a: Volumetric light is the visible beam. Dust motes are the specks inside it. You can have a shaft with smooth haze, or a shaft with countable motes; the mote look insists on the specks.

faq.q: When should I use Dust Motes?
faq.a: Use them when stillness should still be alive: closed rooms, late sun, churches. Do not fill the entire volume, and do not substitute fire sparks.

faq.q: How do I prompt Dust Motes for AI image or video?
faq.a: Put specks in a shaft, not soup in a room. Example: dust motes hanging in a shaft of light around [Subject], slow particles, a room that has been closed. Dark surround, backlight, no fog fill.

title: Dust and Sand
narrative: A rider is a cutout. The sun is a disk you can look at.
Grit crawls across metal and teeth. This is not a poetic far ridge.
This is the ground in the lungs. Use it when the environment is an antagonist: border desert, convoy, siege.
It is the wrong tool when you only need paler mountains behind a sharp hero ( Atmospheric Haze ). It is the wrong tool when the particles hang in a quiet indoor shaft ( Dust Motes ).
Hard Light through a storm becomes a brown disk; do not keep a crisp white sun and a clean face unless the storm is still on the way.
how: Fill near and mid air with wind-driven particulates (fuller's earth, practical sand, or digital grit) so contrast collapses at working distance. Keep a strong directional wind.
Backlight or sun-through-dust to silhouette. Let highlights on skin and vehicles pick up specks.
Prompt: dust or sandstorm wrapping [Subject], sun as a dull coin, silhouettes, grit in the highlights.
when: Use it for an ambush, a crossing, a road that should be unsurvivable. Do not use it as a warm grade on a calm dune.
If flags hang limp and pores are clean, there is no storm.
vs: Atmospheric Haze is calm aerial perspective over kilometers, subject still sharp. Fog is water, grey-white, little wind required.
Smoke has a fire source. Hard Light is the sun's character; in a storm that sun is filtered.
Dust-storm is mineral, windy, and near.
examples_film: Sicario lets desert particulate erase edges and turn daylight hostile. Mad Max: Fury Road drives through walls of grit and sun as a coin.
Lawrence of Arabia also uses blowing sand as an attack, not only distant haze. Use wind and near opacity, not a tan LUT.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Atmospheric Haze (sharp rider, paler citadel) or a brown grade. The tell: clean pores, limp flags, a white sun, crisp horizon.
The fix: wind, near-air grit, silhouettes, a dull solar disk, specks on highlights.

faq.q: What is Dust and Sand in film?
faq.a: Dust and sand as a storm is wind-driven mineral in the air, dense enough to silhouette figures and turn the sun into a dull coin. The land occupies the near optical path.

faq.q: Dust and Sand vs Atmospheric Haze
faq.a: Haze pales far planes and leaves the subject sharp. A dust storm attacks the near ground, reduces visibility, and needs wind. One is distance; the other is an assault.

faq.q: When should I use Dust and Sand?
faq.a: Use it when the land should attack: crossings, convoys, sieges. Do not use it as a warm filter on a still desert portrait.

faq.q: How do I prompt Dust and Sand for AI image or video?
faq.a: Ask for wind-driven grit and a dull sun. Example: dust or sandstorm wrapping [Subject], sun as a dull coin, silhouettes, grit in the highlights. Demand dirty air at working distance.

title: Fog
narrative: A sodium lamp becomes a ball. A platform ends in nothing.
A coat arrives late, as if the world were only as large as a flashlight. Hide geography.
Delay the reveal. Use it for horror, docks, London streets, any beat that should withhold the next plane.
It is the wrong tool when you still want kilometers of readable landscape: that is Atmospheric Haze . It is the wrong tool when the veil is thin and lyrical: that is Mist .
Combustion with a source is Smoke . If faces at three meters are crisp and only the grade is grey, you do not have fog.
You have a LUT.
how: Fill a volume with dense droplets (machines or weather) so contrast falls with distance on a short scale. Backlight or sidelight the fog to make globes around practicals; front light flattens it to milk.
Keep practicals inside the soup, not only a filter on the lens. Prompt: dense fog around [Subject], depth collapsing, lamps becoming globes, figures appearing late, horror or London grammar.
when: Use it when a figure should appear late, a road should end in white, a house should have no yard. Do not use it on a vista you still need to read.
If the far ridge must stay a ridge, use haze or mist.
vs: Mist is thinner: layered, see-through, lyric. Atmospheric Haze stacks paler planes over kilometers, not a wall at ten meters.
Smoke has a source and a direction and is not weather. Steam rises from heat and thins as it cools.
Fog is a local, dense water veil.
examples_film: The Exorcist and The Others use fog to withhold houses, lamps, and bodies. Sicario lets dust and fog-like veils erase desert edges (a cousin in opacity).
Use delayed reveal and globes around lamps, not a copied graveyard.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Atmospheric Haze (distance) or a desaturated grade. The tell: sharp buildings a block away, lamps with no globes, faces fully lit at thirty meters.
The fix: short visibility, backlit bloom on lights, late arrivals.

faq.q: What is Fog in film?
faq.a: Fog is a dense local cloud of water droplets that hides depth. Lamps bloom into globes and figures appear only when they enter the near ground.

faq.q: Fog vs Mist
faq.a: Fog is opaque enough to collapse geography at short range. Mist is thinner, layered, and still lets you read the next plane. Fog withholds; mist veils.

faq.q: When should I use Fog?
faq.a: Use it to hide geography and delay a reveal. Do not use it when you need a long, readable landscape, and do not fake it with a grey LUT.

faq.q: How do I prompt Fog for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the soup and the bloom. Example: dense fog around [Subject], lamps becoming globes, figures appearing late. Give a short visibility distance and forbid crisp far detail.

title: Atmospheric Haze
narrative: A citadel sits in a paler key than the rider. The next cliff is paler still.
Show kilometers, not just meters. Depth is weather, not a second fog machine at the actor's feet.

Use it for desert, city, sea, any wide that must recede. It is the wrong tool when the next person should vanish at five meters ( Fog ) or when you want a shaft you can cut with a hand ( Volumetric Light in a smoky room).
Haze is aerial perspective, not a local veil. If the foreground is milky, you hazed the lens, not the distance.
how: Keep the near ground relatively clean. Let successive planes lift in value, lose contrast, and often shift toward the sky color.
Dust, humidity, or pollution can be real; a graded aerial perspective can stand in if the physics hold. Hard sun through haze becomes a disk.
Prompt: atmospheric haze stacking distance around [Subject], aerial perspective, far planes paler, depth as weather.
when: Use it on a ridge, a skyline, a valley, a megacity grid. Do not use it to hide a monster in a corridor.
If the scare is in the room, use fog, smoke, or darkness.
vs: Mist is local layered moisture at human distances. Fog is dense and near.
Volumetric Light is a beam made visible by particles, often indoors. Dust and Sand is wind-driven grit that attacks the near ground too.
Haze leaves the subject sharp and sends the world backward.
examples_film: Lawrence of Arabia lets desert distance go paler until armies are weather. Blade Runner 2049 stacks orange and pale planes so the city has kilometers.
Use successive paler ridges, not a fogged close-up.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Fog on the actor, or a low-contrast grade on every plane. The tell: the face is milky, or the far citadel is as sharp as the horse.
The fix: sharp near, paler far, several stacked distances, particles too small to resolve.

faq.q: What is Atmospheric Haze in film?
faq.a: Atmospheric haze is air scattering over long distance. Far planes go paler and lower in contrast while the near subject stays readable, so kilometers become visible.

faq.q: Atmospheric Haze vs Mist
faq.a: Mist is a local, often wet veil at walking distances. Haze is aerial perspective over kilometers. Mist can wet your coat; haze pales a mountain range.

faq.q: When should I use Atmospheric Haze?
faq.a: Use it when a wide must recede: desert, city, sea, valley. Do not use it to hide a figure in a room.

faq.q: How do I prompt Atmospheric Haze for AI image or video?
faq.a: Keep the subject sharp and pale the distance. Example: atmospheric haze stacking distance around [Subject], far planes paler. Name successive ridges or blocks of city, not a fog bank at the lens.

title: Mist
narrative: Ridges stack as paler copies of themselves. A horse is readable, then a second ridge, then a paler third.
Softer mystery than fog. Lyric, not monster.
Use it for dawn, river valleys, high cold air, a courtyard that should glow rather than vanish. It is the wrong tool when a killer should appear at two meters with no yard behind them: that is Fog .
It is the wrong tool when the paleness is only far, far away over desert: that is Atmospheric Haze . If you cannot see the subject at all, you overshot into fog.
If every plane is equally sharp, you have no mist.
how: Use a light density of droplets or a real inversion layer. Backlight the layers so each plane separates (aerial perspective at short-to-medium range).
Keep contrast on the near subject; let receding planes lift in value and lose saturation. Prompt: light mist around [Subject], softer than fog, morning or mountain breath, layers of pale air.
when: Use it for a hunt at dawn, a mountain pass, a wet garden. Do not use it as horror soup, and do not fill an interior with it unless the windows are open on a cold morning.
Interiors with volume are often Smoke or haze juice, not mist.
vs: Fog hides. Atmospheric Haze is scattering over long distance, often without local wetness on skin.
Smoke has a source. Rain falls.
Mist hangs, layers, and remains see-through at working distance.
examples_film: The Revenant uses morning and mountain moisture as stacked pale planes around bodies. Raise the Red Lantern lets courtyard air go milky without erasing architecture.
Use layered breath, not a white-out.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Fog (too dense) or Atmospheric Haze (only the horizon pales). The tell: the hero vanishes, or only the skyline is pale while mid-ground is hard.
The fix: keep the subject readable, stack two or three paler planes, backlight the moisture.

faq.q: What is Mist in film?
faq.a: Mist is a light suspension of water droplets that layers the air without erasing the subject. It is thicker than clear air and thinner than fog.

faq.q: Mist vs Fog
faq.a: Fog collapses depth at short range and delays figures. Mist leaves the near ground readable and stacks pale planes. One is a wall; the other is breath.

faq.q: When should I use Mist?
faq.a: Use it for morning, mountains, and lyric distance at human scale. Do not use it when geography must disappear for a scare.

faq.q: How do I prompt Mist for AI image or video?
faq.a: Ask for layered pale air and a readable subject. Example: light mist around [Subject], softer than fog, morning or mountain breath. Specify backlight and forbid a white-out.

title: Ocean
narrative: A mole, a boat, a body: small. The horizon is a line that can kill you.
Swell has a period. Salt in backlight is weather.
The sea is the other actor. Use it for exile, work, awe, war at the rail.
It is the wrong tool when you have left the surface ( Underwater ). It is the wrong tool when the water is a still lake used as silk behind a posed figure.
If there is no swell and no scale, it is not ocean. A bathtub, a pool, a harbor with no fetch: different jobs.
Name the swell.
how: Shoot wide enough for scale. Put real swell in the frame (period, whitecaps or long rollers).
Backlight spray. Let far water go paler with Atmospheric Haze .
Keep the human or boat small unless the story is a face against a rail. Practical water on lens is allowed; fake silk water is not.
Prompt: ocean world of [Subject], swell, horizon, salt light, a person against water that does not care.
when: Use it when the sea must act: a crossing, a lighthouse rock, a mole under fire, a diver's surface world. Do not use it as a backdrop for fashion on calm glass.
If the camera goes under, switch techniques.
vs: Underwater submerges the lens. Atmospheric Haze is the aerial perspective over the water, a modifier, not the whole job.
Rain can lash a surface but is not swell. Ocean is surface gravity, horizon, and scale.
A wet street is not an ocean.
examples_film: The Big Blue treats the surface as a workplace and a temptation. The Lighthouse puts two men against water and rock with no kindness in the horizon.
Dunkirk uses mole, hull, and swell as hostile architecture. Show weight and weather, not a stock seascape.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a calm stock seascape or Underwater caustics on a dry beach. The tell: no swell, a posed model large in frame, glass-smooth water, no spray.
The fix: scale the human down, give the sea a period, backlight salt, keep the horizon honest.

faq.q: What is Ocean in film?
faq.a: Ocean work puts a person or boat against real swell and a horizon, with salt light and spray in the air. The sea is an actor, not a backdrop.

faq.q: Ocean vs Underwater
faq.a: Ocean is the surface world: sky, swell, horizon. Underwater submerges the camera and loses that horizon. One is weather and scale; the other is a different medium.

faq.q: When should I use Ocean?
faq.a: Use it when the sea must act on a body, a boat, or a rock. Do not use a still lake or a pool, and do not stay in ocean grammar once the lens has left the air.

faq.q: How do I prompt Ocean for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name swell, horizon, and scale. Example: ocean world of [Subject], swell, horizon, salt light, a person against water that does not care. Demand period in the waves and backlight on spray.

title: Rain
narrative: Silver needles between a lamp and the lens. Shoulders darken.
Puddles double the neon. Weather is percussion you can see.
Make the air visible and the ground reflective. Use it when the scene must be wet in depth, not only on a window pane.
It is the wrong tool when you only need specular streets at night with no falling drops: that is a Wet-Down . It is also the wrong tool when you want a still veil that hides geography: that is Fog .
Rain against a bright overcast sky reads as nothing. Put a light behind the drops, toward camera, or lose the storm.
how: Put water in the air (rain bars, towers, or a real front) and light it from behind or the side so droplets scatter toward the lens. Keep a darkish background so streaks separate.
Wet the ground even if the rain is light. Shutter angle controls streak length versus beads.
Prompt: heavy rain around [Subject], backlit drops, wet-down pavement, umbrellas, silver streaks, weather as percussion.
when: Use it for a night street, a rooftop, a prison yard, any beat that needs falling water as a layer. Do not use it as a grade or as window tracks only.
If the air is empty and the asphalt is merely shiny, you shot a wet-down.
vs: A Wet-Down soaks surfaces so lights double; it need not rain. Atmospheric Haze is a distant scatter, not falling drops.
Snow is ice that settles and accumulates. Fog is a local veil that hides figures.
Rain falls, streaks when backlit, and leaves the ground wet.
examples_film: Blade Runner builds night as backlit rain and reflective streets. Seven uses rain as a constant layer over investigation.
The Shawshank Redemption lets a yard storm become a body-length release. Use drop, backlight, and wet ground, not a copied coat.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Wet-Down (shiny street, empty air) or a blue LUT called rain. The tell: no streaks against lamps, dry shoulders, no puddles.
The fix: put drops in the air, backlight them, wet the ground.

faq.q: What is Rain in film?
faq.a: Rain is falling water used as visible matter: backlit streaks in the air and reflective ground. Both the optical path and the pavement have to be wet.

faq.q: Rain vs Wet-Down
faq.a: A wet-down sprays surfaces so night lights specularize, often with no weather in the air. Rain adds falling drops. You usually wet-down under rain; you can wet-down without rain.

faq.q: When should I use Rain?
faq.a: Use it when air must streak and ground must mirror. Do not use it if you only need a shiny street, and do not expect rain to read against a bright empty sky without backlight.

faq.q: How do I prompt Rain for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name backlit drops and wet ground. Example: heavy rain around [Subject], backlit drops, wet-down pavement, silver streaks. Specify the lamp behind the rain and forbid dry asphalt.

title: Smoke
narrative: A practical lamp becomes a wedge through grey air. A drag on a cigarette writes a ribbon.
Photograph the air of a room. The walls were always there; now the air is too.
Use it when volume should be visible indoors or when a battle, a chimney, or a club must have a source. It is the wrong tool when the veil is weather with no fire ( Fog , Mist ).
It is the wrong tool when the white stuff rises off a manhole because water met cold air: that is Steam . Without a key or backlight, smoke is only a smell.
Front-filling a room with unlit smoke turns faces to mud.
how: Pick a source and a particle (cigarette, incense, oil, battlefield pot). Control air currents so ribbons have direction.
Light from the side or behind so the volume renders; use a hard beam if you want shafts ( Volumetric Light ). Keep some clean path to the face.
Prompt: smoke around [Subject], cigarette, chimney, or battle, shafts of light catching it, volume in the room.
when: Use it for apartments, temples, engine rooms, aftermath. Do not use it as a default 'atmosphere' pass on a sunny kitchen.
If the beat is stillness in a closed parlor, Dust Motes in a shaft may be enough.
vs: Atmospheric Haze in the distance is aerial perspective. A hazer used to fill a stage is a cousin of smoke but without a story source; still light it as volume.
Fog is wet weather. Steam is water vapor from heat, white, rising, condensing.
Dust Motes are discrete specks in a beam, not a ribbon.
examples_film: In the Mood for Love lets cigarette ribbons occupy cramped rooms. Blade Runner fills interiors so shafts and practicals have air to hit.
Apocalypse Now makes battle and jungle air into volume. Give smoke a source and a light, not a generic grey.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Fog (no source) or unlit fill that dirties skin. The tell: no chimney or cigarette, lamps without shafts, a muddy key.
The fix: a visible source, side or back light, a clean path to the eyes.

faq.q: What is Smoke in film?
faq.a: Smoke is airborne combustion particles from a source, dense enough that light can carve the room's air into volume. It has direction, swirls, and a reason to exist.

faq.q: Smoke vs Atmospheric Haze
faq.a: Haze pales distant planes over kilometers. Smoke occupies a room or a battlefield and needs a source and a sculpting light. One is distance; the other is volume you could walk through.

faq.q: When should I use Smoke?
faq.a: Use it to photograph a room's air, a chimney, a cigarette, a battle. Do not use it as weather, and do not fill a face with unlit particles.

faq.q: How do I prompt Smoke for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name source and lighting. Example: smoke around [Subject], cigarette, chimney, or battle, shafts of light catching it. Demand a readable face and visible volume, not a grey grade.

title: Snow
narrative: Flakes cross a sodium lamp like slow sparks that do not burn. Shoulders collect white.
Footsteps write the path. Hush the world.
Silence becomes visible as reduced contrast and falling matter. Use it when winter must occupy both air and ground.
It is the wrong tool when you only need pale air without accumulation ( Mist ). It is the wrong tool when the falling matter is liquid ( Rain ).
Rain wets and mirrors; snow blankets and records tracks. Tiny fast specks against a day sky read as video noise.
Size the flakes and backlight them.
how: Put flakes in the air (practical or digital) large enough to read, and light them from behind or the side. Let accumulation sit on wool, hair, rails, and ground.
Keep a dark background for flakes to separate, or accept a white-on-white hush. Wind decides drift versus fall.
Prompt: falling snow around [Subject], large flakes in backlight, muffled world, tracks, winter silence you can see.
when: Use it for a platform wait, a hunt, a small-town crime, a night street that should go quiet. Do not use it as white rain that never settles.
If shoulders stay dry and the pavement is only wet, you shot rain.
vs: Rain streaks and mirrors. Mist hangs and does not accumulate as a blanket.
Blue Hour is a sky condition that often pairs with snow but is not weather. Dust Motes are indoor specks in a shaft.
Snow falls, lands, and stays.
examples_film: Fargo lets snow be ground, air, and isolation. Let the Right One In uses falling flakes and muffled suburbs.
The Revenant puts bodies into falling and settled winter. Use accumulation and backlight, not a noise overlay.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Rain tinted white, or grain called snow. The tell: wet mirrors, no accumulation, specks too small to size.
The fix: large backlit flakes, settled white on surfaces, tracks, a hush in contrast.

faq.q: What is Snow in film?
faq.a: Snow is ice in the air and on the ground: backlit flakes, accumulation, tracks, a quieter contrast. It occupies volume and records passage.

faq.q: Snow vs Rain
faq.a: Rain is liquid: streaks, splashes, mirrors. Snow is crystal: drift, settle, blanket. If the street specularizes and coats stay dark, you are still in rain.

faq.q: When should I use Snow?
faq.a: Use it when winter should hush the world and leave tracks. Do not use it as white rain, and do not omit accumulation.

faq.q: How do I prompt Snow for AI image or video?
faq.a: Specify large backlit flakes and settled white. Example: falling snow around [Subject], large flakes in backlight, muffled world, tracks. Demand accumulation on wool and ground.

title: Sparks and Embers
narrative: A welder writes a fountain. A collapsing floor throws embers that hang, then die.
Industry or apocalypse in the air. Unlike dust, these specks have temperature and a brief life.

Use it when the air should be dangerous or industrial: a foundry, a burning street, a cigarette in a dark booth (embers, not a fountain). It is the wrong tool when the specks are cold ( Dust Motes , Snow ).

It is the wrong tool when the glow is only a warm key on a face with no particles: that is Candlelight or firelight without weather. If the particles are large, slow, and white, you probably asked for snow.
If they never fall, you asked for hanging dust.
how: Give them a source (welder, angle grinder, timber, cigarette). Let gravity and heat dictate: sparks drop and bounce; embers can loft and drift.
Expose for the particle without losing the face entirely, or accept silhouettes. A dark surround makes them read.
Prompt: sparks or embers around [Subject], welding, fire, cigarettes, orange particles as weather.
when: Use it for a night burn, a factory, a ruined city, a match. Do not sprinkle orange specks on a pastoral wide with no fire.
Particles need a reason.
vs: Candlelight is a warm, flickering key. Sparks are the particles.
Volumetric Light is a shaft; sparks can cross it but are not the shaft. Dust Motes are cold and slow in a beam.
Snow is cold and accumulates. Sparks die in the air.
examples_film: Blade Runner 2049 throws orange particles as industrial weather. The Dark Knight Rises uses fire and debris as airborne specks in night action.
Use source plus trajectory, not a spark overlay on a clean street.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Dust Motes tinted orange, or Snow . The tell: specks hang forever, accumulate on the ground as white, or have no welder or fire.
The fix: a hot source, brief trajectories, self-luminous particles, dark air.

faq.q: What is Sparks and Embers in film?
faq.a: Sparks and embers are burning particles in the air, thrown by welding, fire, or a cigarette. They light themselves, follow short trajectories, and die.

faq.q: Sparks and Embers vs Dust Motes
faq.a: Dust motes are cold specks in a shaft of light. Sparks are incandescent and come from a hot source. One is time in a closed room; the other is industry or fire.

faq.q: When should I use Sparks and Embers?
faq.a: Use them when the air should carry heat: welding, collapse, a cigarette coal. Do not sprinkle orange dots on a scene with no fire.

faq.q: How do I prompt Sparks and Embers for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the hot source and the trajectories. Example: sparks or embers around [Subject], welding, fire, cigarettes, orange particles as weather. Dark surround, gravity, no snow.

title: Steam
narrative: A locomotive writes a column that the platform wind tears. A manhole breathes.
A shower erases a body in white. Heat meeting cold air.
Industrial or intimate, the physics are the same. Use it when the source is hot water or hot metal in cold space.
It is the wrong tool when the cloud is burning ( Smoke ) or hanging as weather ( Fog ). Smoke can sink and stain; steam wants to rise and vanish.
If the white cloud has no grate, kettle, train, or shower, you have fog in a trench coat.
how: Show the source (stack, manhole, shower head, kettle). Let the vapor rise and shear in wind.
Backlight for a white, translucent volume; it should feel wetter and brighter than smoke. Condensation on glass and wool helps.
Prompt: steam billowing around [Subject], trains, manholes, showers, a white veil, industrial or intimate heat.
when: Use it on a winter platform, a night street grate, a bathroom, a factory press. Do not use it as generic alley 'atmosphere' with no heat.
If the alley is burning, use smoke. If the alley is only wet and cold, use fog or rain.
vs: Smoke is combustion, often grey or colored, with a fire source. Fog is ambient water droplets without a hot origin.
Atmospheric Haze is distant scatter. Steam is a thermal event: white, rising, local to a grate, stack, or shower.
examples_film: Winter station grammar in thrillers leans on locomotive steam as moving architecture. The Untouchables uses train steam as a white, violent veil.
Drive lets night streets breathe from grates. Spirited Away treats bathhouse steam as a wet interior weather.
Show the heat, not a smoke bomb.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Smoke (wrong color, wrong source) or Fog (no rise from heat). The tell: a grey cloud sitting still with no grate or stack.
The fix: a thermal source, white translucent rise, backlight, wind shear.

faq.q: What is Steam in film?
faq.a: Steam is water vapor from heat meeting colder air. It billows from trains, manholes, showers, and kettles: a white, wet, rising veil with a thermal source.

faq.q: Steam vs Smoke
faq.a: Smoke is combustion particles and can hang, stain, and go grey. Steam is wet vapor, brighter, rising, tied to heat and cold air. One burns; the other boils.

faq.q: When should I use Steam?
faq.a: Use it when heat and cold air are in the scene: platforms, grates, baths, presses. Do not use it as a generic alley cloud with no source.

faq.q: How do I prompt Steam for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the hot source and the white rise. Example: steam billowing around [Subject], trains, manholes, showers, a white veil. Backlight it and keep it wetter than smoke.

title: Underwater
narrative: Hair and cloth delay. Light arrives as moving lattice from a surface that is now a ceiling.
There is no standing horizon, only up toward silver and down toward dark. Leave air.

Use it when the scene is actually submerged: a pool, a sea, a tank, a flood. It is the wrong tool when you only want grace: dry Slow Motion with a blue grade is a lie, and it shows in hair that still falls at air speed.
It is the wrong tool when the story is on the swell with a sky: that is Ocean . Color dies with depth (reds first).
If the red dress is still loud at ten meters, you stayed in air.
how: Put the lens in a housing in water (or a convincing tank). Expose for caustics from the real sun or a hard source through the surface.
Let bubbles and silt backlight. Wardrobe and hair must float.
Camera moves fight drag; they read slower. Prompt: underwater of [Subject], caustics, muffled space, hair and cloth in slow water, a world without horizon.
when: Use it for a dive, a drowning, a creature, a flooded corridor. Do not use it as a look for a dry bedroom.
If you need the surface and the sky, shoot ocean, then go under for a beat if the story dives.
vs: Ocean is the surface world: swell, horizon, salt light. Atmospheric Haze is air scatter.
Slow Motion is a frame-rate choice that often accompanies underwater but is not the medium. Underwater is a different optical path: refraction, caustics, buoyancy, no air horizon.
examples_film: The Big Blue lives in the medium, not in a tint. The Shape of Water makes tanks and canals a second gravity.
Thunderball proved action can be staged as true submerged geography. Use caustics and float, not a teal LUT on a dry actor.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a blue grade in air, or Ocean from a boat. The tell: cloth hangs, hair falls, a skyline, no caustics.
The fix: submerge the camera, float the fabrics, add caustics and backlit silt, kill the air horizon.

faq.q: What is Underwater in film?
faq.a: Underwater work puts camera and subject in water, so caustics, buoyancy, particles, and a missing air horizon rewrite the frame. The medium is the atmosphere.

faq.q: Underwater vs Ocean
faq.a: Ocean is the surface: swell, sky, a horizon that can kill you. Underwater leaves that sky and treats the surface as a ceiling. One is a seascape; the other is a different world.

faq.q: When should I use Underwater?
faq.a: Use it when the scene is submerged. Do not use a blue grade or slow motion in air as a substitute, and do not call a boat horizon underwater.

faq.q: How do I prompt Underwater for AI image or video?
faq.a: Demand caustics, floating cloth, and no air horizon. Example: underwater of [Subject], caustics, muffled space, hair and cloth in slow water. Specify silt or bubbles in backlight.

title: Wet-Down
narrative: Sodium, neon, a traffic headlamp: each finds a second copy on blacktop. Night exteriors that must sparkle.
Studio crews invented this because dry asphalt eats light. The trick is the shine, not the storm.
Use it when a night street, alley, or overpass must specularize practicals. It is the wrong tool when you need falling streaks and umbrellas as percussion: add Rain .

It is the wrong tool when the color should come only from tubes on walls with a dry floor: that is Neon Practicals without a mirror. If the air is full of drops, you have rain (usually on top of a wet-down).
If the air is empty and the ground is a black mirror, you have the wet-down alone.
how: Hose or rain-bar the travel path until it sheets. Place practicals (sodium, neon, shop windows) so their reflections fall in frame.
Keep the camera low enough to catch the mirror, or lose it. No need for backlight in the air unless rain is also falling.
Prompt: wet-down streets around [Subject], pavement sprayed for night, double the lights by reflection.
when: Use it for night driving, a sidewalk wait, a neon block. Do not soak a dusty noon street unless the story has just rained.
A wet-down in hard sun can look like a spill, not night grammar.
vs: Rain puts drops in the optical path. Neon Practicals is the source color; wet-down is how that color doubles on the ground.
Fog blooms lamps in air. Wet-down blooms them on the floor.
Atmospheric Haze does not spec the asphalt.
examples_film: Drive and Collateral make Los Angeles nights out of wet asphalt and practicals. Who Framed Roger Rabbit's night streets use the same studio-wet logic so lamps have copies.
Use the mirror, not a copied car.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Rain (streaks in air) or a glossy grade on dry pavement. The tell: drops around lamps, or no reflections despite 'wet streets.' The fix: sheet the ground, place lights that can reflect, keep air empty if rain is not the job.

faq.q: What is Wet-Down in film?
faq.a: A wet-down is a sprayed street or surface that turns night practicals into reflections. It is a ground treatment. Rain is optional.

faq.q: Wet-Down vs Rain
faq.a: Rain is weather in the air. Wet-down is water on the ground so lights double. Night work often uses both; they are not the same request.

faq.q: When should I use Wet-Down?
faq.a: Use it when a night exterior must sparkle from the pavement. Do not use it as a substitute for falling rain, and do not soak a dry noon scene without a story reason.

faq.q: How do I prompt Wet-Down for AI image or video?
faq.a: Ask for sprayed pavement and reflected practicals. Example: wet-down streets around [Subject], pavement sprayed for night, double the lights by reflection. Specify empty air if you do not want rain.

title: Bird's-Eye View
narrative: From up there the body is a token. Circulation, grouping, and the shape of a courtyard or a table take over.

You use it to turn a fight, a dinner, or a street into a pattern the participants cannot see. The camera is high enough that the floor is the picture, but unlike a close Overhead Top-Down you still feel drop: altitude, not a light stand over a desk.
It is the wrong tool when you need a face, a line of dialogue, or a simple sense that someone is small in a room. That last job is often a High Angle from a balcony.
If the model flies and tours, you have left the still viewpoint for a drone move.
how: Place the camera well above the action and pitch it steeply down, approaching 70 to 90 degrees. Great height is required: a ceiling corner of a lobby, a crane, a rooftop, a high grid.
Anatomy foreshortens; heads and shoulders become discs. Keep extra limbs out of a seated tableau or the map grows a mutant.
Light from above will flatten; a raking key throws shadows as drawing on the floor. Prompt: bird's-eye straight down from a great height, floor as a map, no extra limbs.
when: Use it to turn life into a board game or a ritual. Concrete beat: one seated person and a table seen from the ceiling so plates and hands are the story.
Do not use it as a sightseeing flyover when the beat is still a person.
vs: High Angle looks down obliquely; the face remains a face. Overhead Top-Down is a 90-degree top-down, often closer, a flat-lay or room plan whose tabletop must stay rectangular.
Crane Over is the path that can arrive at a bird's-eye. Aerial and FPV Drone add flight; bird's-eye can be a locked steep look.
examples_film: The Grand Budapest Hotel uses steep downward views so hotels, desks, and ceremonies read as designed diagrams. Requiem for a Dream looks down until apartments and bodies are patterns of habit.
Use the altitude and the map, not a copied lobby.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a mild High Angle (too little height) or a close Overhead Top-Down (too little altitude, too much product photography). Tell: a readable standing portrait from a step-stool, or a desk filling the frame with no drop.
Fix: camera high above, looking steeply down, bodies foreshortened, floor as geography. Ban extra arms in seated groups.

faq.q: What is bird's-eye view in film?
faq.a: A bird's-eye view looks steeply or straight down from a great height. People and furniture become a map; altitude is the viewpoint.

faq.q: Bird's-eye view vs overhead
faq.a: Bird's-eye implies great height and a map of a place. Overhead top-down is 90 degrees and often closer: a table, a crime scene, or a dance as a graphic plan.

faq.q: When should I use bird's-eye view?
faq.a: Use it when grouping, ritual, or circulation should win over any one face. Do not use it for dialogue or for a product lying on a table.

faq.q: How do I prompt bird's-eye view for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Bird's-eye view straight down on [Subject] from a great height, floor as a map, bodies foreshortened, no extra limbs. Say not a high-angle portrait and not a 90-degree desk flat-lay.

title: Dutch Angle
narrative: Pitch looks up or down. Roll breaks the floor.

A Dutch (canted, oblique) shot is a choice about gravity, not about power height. Use it when the moral or mental line is already bent: a sick city, a fight that will not stay fair, a mind that cannot stand up.
Adjacent level shots make the cant mean something. If every setup is Dutch, nothing is.
It is not a Low Angle . Looking up with a level roll is a different axis.
It is not a Dutch Roll either: that is the move that rotates into a cant during the shot. A static Dutch is a frozen decision.
how: Rotate the camera around the lens axis. A readable working cant is about 15 to 30 degrees; past 45 the frame often just looks like a mistake.
Compose diagonals on purpose: stair rails, streets, a leaning body that agrees or argues with the roll. Keep the set rigid.
The sensation should come from the viewpoint, not from warped walls. Decide whether the reverse stays level for contrast.
Prompt: Dutch angle, camera rolled 20 to 30 degrees, diagonal horizon.
when: Use it when the world is off its axis. Concrete beat: a stairwell confrontation, banister as a diagonal, both feet still planted on real steps.
Do not use it as decoration on every villain or every night street.
vs: Eye Level with a level horizon is the control condition. Incline is a gentler cant, a few degrees of slope rather than a full lean.
Dutch Roll and Camera Roll are motion on this axis. Low Angle pitches up; High Angle pitches down.
Neither is a Dutch until you also roll.
examples_film: The Third Man cants Vienna's streets and encounters so the postwar city will not sit true. Do the Right Thing angles selected confrontations rather than the whole film.
Mission: Impossible uses canted Prague coverage; the later rotating vault is a different trick (the set moves). Borrow a motivated static roll, not a permanent lean.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Low Angle (pitch) or a moving Dutch Roll . Tell: ceiling in frame but horizon level, or the camera rotating during the shot when you wanted a still lean.
Fix: level pitch, roll 20 to 30 degrees, lock it. The other failure is 60-degree decoration on every setup.
If the next shot is also canted, the cant has no contrast.

faq.q: What is a Dutch angle in film?
faq.a: A Dutch angle rolls the camera so the horizon and verticals tilt. The frame's relationship to gravity is broken on purpose, usually as a static cant.

faq.q: Dutch angle vs low angle
faq.a: A low angle pitches the camera up from below the eyes. A Dutch angle rolls the camera; the floor slants. You can combine them, but they are different axes.

faq.q: When should I use a Dutch angle?
faq.a: Use it when disequilibrium, aggression, or a stylized sick world should be in the geometry. Do not use it as a default mood for night or villains.

faq.q: How do I prompt a Dutch angle for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Dutch angle of [Subject], camera rolled 20 to 30 degrees, diagonal horizon, static cant, walls not warped. Say it is not a low angle and not a rolling camera.

title: Eye Level
narrative: Rank in a frame comes from where the lens sits and how it is pitched. Eye-level refuses that assignment.
Two people at matching eye height read as peers; the room does not look down on them, and they do not loom. Sit when they sit.
Stand when they stand. The judgment, if any, has to come from performance, costume, or light, not from geometry.
It is the wrong tool when the beat is surveillance, monument, or a map. A few degrees of pitch and you have already cut to a High Angle or a Low Angle .
A few inches down and you are in Shoulder Level , which is a companion, not a peer.
how: Match the nodal point to the subject's eyes. Keep roll at zero so verticals stay vertical.

A 35mm to 50mm keeps perspective close to human vision; a wide from the same height will still stretch the room without changing rank. Height and tilt are independent: a camera at eye height that looks down is no longer an eye-level shot, it is a high angle from eye height.
Prompt it as camera at their eye height, horizon level, no tilt up or down.
when: Use it for a conversation that should not take sides, or for a face you want believed without the camera lobbying. Concrete beat: two adults at a kitchen table, seated eyes matched, no ceiling grab.
Do not look down or up unless you mean it.
vs: High Angle pitches down and shrinks the figure. Low Angle pitches up and grows it.
Shoulder Level sits a few inches below the eyes, like a walking companion. Point of View is what the character sees, not a camera beside them at the same height.
Over-the-Shoulder Coverage keeps a near body in the foreground; eye-level can be a clean Single .
examples_film: Tokyo Story holds domestic talk at human height so posture, not a power tilt, does the judging. Rosetta stays with her at her own eye line as she moves, refusing a look down.
Use those as grammar: match height to the person in the scene, keep the horizon honest.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a mild Low Angle , because generators treat a portrait as a poster. Tell: ceiling in frame, chin from below, verticals converging.
Fix: camera at eye height, horizon level, no tilt. If the subject is seated, sit the camera; standing eye-level on a seated person is already looking down.

faq.q: What is eye level in film?
faq.a: An eye-level shot places the camera at the subject's eye height with a level horizon. The sightline is horizontal, so the frame does not assign power by looking up or down.

faq.q: Eye level vs high angle
faq.a: Eye level matches the subject's eyes and stays level. A high-angle shot raises the camera and pitches it down, so more floor enters and the figure occupies less of the rectangle.

faq.q: When should I use eye level?
faq.a: Use it when the relationship should read as equal: talk, witness, default coverage. Skip it when the beat needs vulnerability from above or monument from below.

faq.q: How do I prompt eye level for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Eye-level shot of [Subject], camera at their eye height, horizon level, no tilt up or down. Name sit versus stand so the model does not look down on a seated body.

title: First-Person
narrative: The audience is the character for a stretch of time. Lady in the Lake tries to tell a detective story this way.
Hardcore Henry runs it as an action body. Enter the Void keeps the camera inside a consciousness that still has a path through rooms.

Hands, a steering wheel, a gun, a door handled at the edge: those are the tells that a person, not an invisible observer, is looking. A Point of View shot can be one cut of what they see, clean of the owner.
First-person keeps the owner as a felt body. Object POV parents the camera to a prop instead.
SnorriCam looks at their face from their chest, which is the opposite ownership.
how: Parent the camera to the character's head or upper chest with a human field of view (roughly 24mm to 35mm spherical, not a tiny action-cam unless that is diegetic). Allow hands, shoulders at the extreme edge, or a tool to enter.
Add breath and footfall as camera motion only as much as a body would. Do not show the owner's face except in glass.
Prompt: first-person camera as [Subject] would see, hands entering frame, breath, a body that owns the lens.
when: Use it when the audience must be the character, not merely glance as them. Concrete beat: running a wet overpass, gloved hands hitting the rail, breath in the cold, no face of the runner.
Do not use it for a two-shot argument; you will lose the listener.
vs: Point of View is the optical slice of the seen world, often an insert after a look, owner body forbidden. Object POV is a ball, a bullet, a phone, a vehicle.
Over-the-Shoulder Coverage keeps us behind someone we can still see. Fourth Wall has them look at us.
SnorriCam bolts the camera to the torso and stares at their face while the world slides.
examples_film: Hardcore Henry keeps the body in the lens: hands, weapons, impacts. Enter the Void rides a consciousness through space after the body is gone, still as a moving first-person path.
Lady in the Lake (1947) attempts extended first-person detective storytelling, other characters addressing the lens as Marlowe. Use those as embodiment grammar.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a clean Point of View plate (no hands) or a Follow Shot behind the actor. Tell: a back of a head, or a perfectly disembodied lock-off of a room.
Fix: hands or a tool in frame, motion as a walk or a turn of the head, owner invisible as a face. If the camera is bolted to a car hood with chrome in frame, you wanted Object POV .

faq.q: What is first-person camera in film?
faq.a: First-person makes the camera a character's body: we see as they see, with hands, breath, or tools entering the frame. It is continuous embodiment, not only a glance.

faq.q: First-person vs POV
faq.a: A POV shot is what they see, often a single insert with no owner body. First-person keeps a body owning the lens over time: hands, locomotion, breath.

faq.q: When should I use first-person?
faq.a: Use it when the audience should inhabit a body for a passage of action or perception. Do not use it for ordinary reverse-shot dialogue.

faq.q: How do I prompt first-person for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: First-person camera as [Subject] would see, hands entering frame, breath, a body that owns the lens. For video, move as they move, tools at the edges, no owner's face.

title: Fourth Wall
narrative: Theatre named the fourth wall; film breaks it when a Ferris explains the day to us, when a killer in Funny Games checks whether we are still complicit, when Alvy steps out of Annie Hall to argue. The eyeline is the mechanism.
Everything else in the shot can stay naturalistic. The turn is the look into glass.
It is not Point of View (we see what they see). It is not a diary voiceover laid over a face that never finds the lens ( Taxi Driver 's narration can run without a break).
It is close to Interview , except interview eyeline is usually just off-lens, to a listener, while fourth-wall treats us as the partner.
how: Place the camera at the subject's eye height and put their eyeline in the center of the taking lens (or a marked pupil on the matte box). Keep the rest of the blocking honest so the look is the only rupture.
A slight Eye Level three-quarter that then turns into the glass can stage the break as a decision. Prompt: fourth-wall look, eyes into the lens, the scene admitting an audience.
when: Use it when they know we are here: a plan explained to us, a dare, a confession that includes the spectator. Concrete beat: a character pauses in a room, finds the lens, and continues the line to us.
Do not sprinkle random winks; the break has to change the contract of the scene.
vs: Point of View inhabits their look into the world. First-Person is their body seeing; other people may look at camera as if at that body, which is diegetic address, not a break.
Interview aims just off-lens to an offscreen questioner. Profile looks away.
Reverse Angle answers another character, not us.
examples_film: Ferris Bueller 's Day Off lets Ferris comment on his own behavior directly to viewers. Funny Games uses looks (and more) to implicate the spectator.
Annie Hall lets Alvy address the audience and step outside ordinary scene realism. The Office glances at the lens as documentary embarrassment, a softer cousin of the same eyeline.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Interview (eyeline off-lens) or a Point of View of another character (someone looking at the first-person body). Tell: they look past the camera, or we see what they see instead of their eyes.
Fix: pupils on the lens, address to the audience. Voiceover without a look is narration, not this shot.

faq.q: What is fourth wall in film?
faq.a: Breaking the fourth wall means a character looks into the taking lens and admits the audience. The eyeline into the camera is the break.

faq.q: Fourth wall vs POV
faq.a: Fourth wall looks at us. A POV shot is what the character sees in their world. One admits a spectator; the other inhabits a looker.

faq.q: When should I use fourth wall?
faq.a: Use it when the contract of the scene should include the audience: explanation, dare, complicity. Do not use it as a random wink with no change in address.

faq.q: How do I prompt fourth wall for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Fourth-wall look from [Subject], eyes into the lens, eye-level, the scene admitting an audience. Not an interview off-lens look, not a POV of the scenery.

title: Ground Level
narrative: From the dirt, a walk is a sequence of soles. A coat trailing, a wheel, a dropped gun, a snake's view of a street: the floor is the foreground and architecture goes large above it.
Westerns and car films live here because the ground is where decisions land. Worm's-Eye View is the cousin that looks straight up until there is no street, only a zenith.
Low Angle can be shot from the waist and never touch the floor. Hip Level still belongs to hands and holsters.
Ground-level is the pedestal on the boards.
how: Set the camera on a low plate, a sandbag, or a hole so the sensor is centimeters from the ground. A wide lens exaggerates the near boots and the far horizon.
You may look along the floor (track, tire, hem) or tilt up (a coat filling the sky). Keep grit, wet, or dust in the near field; that is how the height reads.
Prompt: ground-level camera, lens nearly on the floor, boots and trailing coat, horizon very low.
when: Use it when the story starts from the dirt: an arrival on foot, a car, a body on the road. Concrete beat: boots stepping onto a dusty street, coat hem in the near field, town rising beyond.
Do not use it as the default for a walking conversation; that is Shoulder Level or Eye Level .
vs: Worm's-Eye View looks sharply up from this height until verticals collapse and the horizon dies. Low Angle is a pitch from below the eyes, not a requirement that the lens kiss the floor.
Hip Level sits at belt height so hands stay in the plane of focus. Overhead Top-Down is the opposite pole: the floor as a plan, not as a foreground.
examples_film: Once Upon a Time in the West lets the station boards, tracks, and boots own the opening; the ground is duration. Drive keeps cars, asphalt, and shoes in the near field so the street is the world.
Borrow the low pedestal and the near-ground texture.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Low Angle from kneeling height with a clean floor and a full face. Tell: no near-ground texture, no boots, camera clearly at knee-plus.
Fix: lens nearly on the floor, grit or pavement sharp in the foreground. If the shot is only nostrils and sky, you drifted into Worm's-Eye View .

faq.q: What is ground level in film?
faq.a: A ground-level shot places the lens almost on the floor. Boots, hems, wheels, and pavement become the near subject; the world rises from the dirt.

faq.q: Ground level vs worm's-eye view
faq.a: Ground level is a height: camera on the floor, often looking along boots or steeply up a coat. Worm's-eye view is an extreme upward pitch from that height, verticals collapsing, almost no street horizon.

faq.q: When should I use ground level?
faq.a: Use it when the ground is part of the beat: a walk, a car, a dropped object, a Western arrival. Do not use it for ordinary seated talk.

faq.q: How do I prompt ground level for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Ground-level camera, lens nearly on the floor, boots and trailing coat in the near field, horizon low. Say whether it looks along the dirt or steeply up.

title: High Angle
narrative: Height plus downward tilt is what assigns the smaller rank. A high angle can be pity, surveillance, or a clinical map of who can reach the door.

The face should still be a face: you see the crown and the shoulders, not only a scalp. Paths and distances that Eye Level would hide become readable because the floor is a diagram with walls still receding.
It is the wrong tool when you need a true plan view. If the tabletop must be a rectangle and bodies become pieces, you wanted Overhead Top-Down or a steep Bird's-Eye View .
It is also the wrong tool for a power confrontation; looking down on the boss fights the line.
how: Raise the camera above the subject's eyes and pitch it down. Typical working range is a step-stool to a short ladder, 20 to 45 degrees of tilt, subject still recognizable through costume and contrast.
Top-light and ceiling practicals become the key more often, because you are now closer to the lights that hang. Keep roll level; a canted high angle is two techniques at once.
Prompt: high-angle shot looking down, figure diminished, more floor than sky, not top-down.
when: Use it for vulnerability, surveillance, or a map of a room that eye-level cannot draw. Concrete beat: a lone figure on a station platform, camera above the lamps, suitcase readable on the boards.
Do not use a high oblique when the shot must be strictly top-down.
vs: Eye Level stays on the sightline and assigns no rank. Bird's-Eye View looks steeply or straight down from a great height until people are a map.
Overhead Top-Down is 90 degrees, a flat-lay or room plan. Low Angle is the opposing pitch.
Crane Over is the move that can arrive at a high or overhead view.
examples_film: Psycho uses a steep high view on the stairway so Arbogast is placed inside the house's geometry before the attack. The Shawshank Redemption uses high views of the prison so human scale sits inside the walls.
Citizen Kane and Prisoners both look down when a person should feel watched or reduced. Borrow the downward pitch and the readable floor, not a poster.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Bird's-Eye View or Overhead Top-Down : the model snaps to a drone plan. Tell: tops of heads only, table as a perfect rectangle, no face.
Fix: looking down 30 degrees, eyes and mouth still readable, walls receding. The other failure is a raised camera that stays level, which is a high vantage, not a high angle.

faq.q: What is a high angle in film?
faq.a: A high-angle shot looks down at the subject from above eye level. The pitch is oblique, so you still read a person, only smaller in their space.

faq.q: High angle vs bird's-eye view
faq.a: A high angle is a downward look that keeps the face and the room in perspective. A bird's-eye view is much higher and steeper, often nearly straight down, until life reads as a map.

faq.q: When should I use a high angle?
faq.a: Use it when someone is vulnerable, watched, or when the floor plan of a room matters more than a power face. Do not use it as a default dramatic portrait.

faq.q: How do I prompt a high angle for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: High-angle shot looking down on [Subject], figure diminished, more floor than ceiling, face still readable, not top-down. Name an approximate tilt if the model keeps flattening the room.

title: Hip Level
narrative: Westerns minted it because a draw happens at the belt. The face is still in the upper frame, but the story is in the fingers, the buckle, the coat hem at the wrist.
Tension reads before anyone looks up. Crime films stole the height for a gun that might come out during a talk.
It is not a Cowboy Shot , which is a frame size from mid-thigh up and can be taken from eye height. It is not a Low Angle unless you also pitch up.
Hip-level can stay level and still make the holster the equator of the picture.
how: Pedestal to belt height on a standing adult (roughly 90 to 110 cm). Keep roll level.
A slight look-up is optional; a true hip-level often aims through the hands toward the far figure. Depth of field should hold the holster and the facing body.
A wider lens at this height will stretch legs; a longer lens compresses the standoff. Prompt: hip-level camera, gunbelt height, hands and holster in the plane of focus.
when: Use it when the hands will decide: a standoff, a pocketed weapon, a key passed at waist height. Concrete beat: two standing figures, belts in a line, fingers idle near leather.
Do not use it when the face is the only event; rise to Shoulder Level or Eye Level .
vs: Cowboy Shot crops mid-thigh as a size; hip-level is where the lens sits. Ground Level is on the dirt and privileges boots.
Low Angle pitches up for monument. Shoulder Level is a walking companion, closer to the face.
Eye Level ignores the belt.
examples_film: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly keeps holsters and hands alive in the line of the lens during standoffs. No Country for Old Men works at belt and pocket height so a captured bolt pistol is as present as a face.
Borrow the height of the hands, not a copied desert.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Low Angle power tilt or a Cowboy Shot from standing eye height. Tell: nostrils and ceiling, or a mid-thigh crop taken from above the chest.
Fix: camera at belt, looking through the hands, horizon level. If only boots are sharp, you dropped to Ground Level .

faq.q: What is hip level in film?
faq.a: A hip-level shot places the camera at belt or holster height. Hands, gait, and weapons sit in the plane of focus; the face remains in the upper frame.

faq.q: Hip level vs cowboy shot
faq.a: Hip level is camera height at the belt. A cowboy shot is a frame size from mid-thigh up. You can combine them, but a cowboy can also be taken from eye height.

faq.q: When should I use hip level?
faq.a: Use it when hands and a possible draw are the beat. Do not use it for a seated talk or a face that needs to fill the frame.

faq.q: How do I prompt hip level for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Hip-level camera on [Subject], gunbelt height, hands and holster in the plane of focus, horizon through the hands, not a low-angle tilt.

title: Incline
narrative: A full Dutch Angle at 20 to 30 degrees is a statement: the axis is broken. Incline is the whisper.

Hallways that should feel 6 to 12 degrees wrong, a street that might be hill or might be mind, a conversation that is not yet a crisis. If the viewer can measure a lean at a glance, you probably overshot into Dutch.
It is still roll, not pitch. A camera looking up a real hill with a level bubble is not an incline; the floor is actually sloped and the frame is true.
Incline cheats gravity in the head, not in the set.
how: Roll the camera a small amount, typically about 5 to 12 degrees, and lock it. Keep architecture readable and bodies upright in the world; only the frame is off.
Do not combine with a wide fisheye or the small cant disappears into distortion. Contrast with a level reverse if you want the incline to be felt.
Prompt: inclined camera, a gentle cant, not a full Dutch, the floor suggesting slope or unease.
when: Use it when a full Dutch is too much and the floor should only suggest slope or unease. Concrete beat: a hotel corridor, 8 degrees of roll, wallpaper still a grid, a person walking toward camera.
Do not use it as a substitute for building a real ramp, and do not park at 25 degrees and call it gentle.
vs: Dutch Angle is the full cant, often 20 to 30 degrees, moral or mental tilt as a graphic. Dutch Roll and Camera Roll move on this axis over time.
Eye Level with a level bubble is the control. Low Angle and High Angle are pitch, not roll.
A real inclined set photographed level is production design, not this technique.
examples_film: The Third Man contains a range of cants; the shallower ones are closer to incline, the harder leans are Dutch. Do the Right Thing similarly varies the amount of roll on confrontations rather than using one angle for every street.
Use degree of roll as a dimmer, not as a single switch.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a full Dutch Angle . Tell: diagonal horizon you could hang a picture on, 25-plus degrees, poster unease.
Fix: 5 to 12 degrees, almost level, a hint of slope. The other failure is pitching up or down and calling it incline.
Check the roll axis: left-right tilt of the horizon, not looking at the ceiling.

faq.q: What is incline in film?
faq.a: An incline is a slight Dutch: a small camera roll so the floor and horizon are a few degrees off true. It suggests slope or unease without a full canted frame.

faq.q: Incline vs Dutch angle
faq.a: A Dutch angle is a clear cant, often 20 to 30 degrees. Incline is gentler, about 5 to 12 degrees, the floor slightly wrong rather than the world off its axis.

faq.q: When should I use incline?
faq.a: Use it when a full Dutch would overstate the beat: a corridor, a talk, a street that should only hint. Do not use it if you need the graphic lean of a true Dutch.

faq.q: How do I prompt incline for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Inclined camera on [Subject], gentle cant about 8 degrees, not a full Dutch, horizon slightly off, walls rigid. Lock the roll; do not roll during the shot unless you want a Dutch roll.

title: Low Angle
narrative: Looking up makes a body into architecture. Door frames, ceiling beams, and the underside of a chin enter the picture.
A boss in a doorway, a statue, a threat: the subject occupies the top of the frame and we occupy the floor. Citizen Kane built ceilings (and sometimes dug a pit) so the look-up had a real lid.
Do not confuse this with a low camera that stays level. A tatami or seated-height camera with a horizontal sightline is a height choice, close to seated Eye Level , not a low angle.
Ozu's rooms sit low without turning the family into towers. If you pitch up on that setup, you have changed the sentence.
It is the wrong tool for a peer conversation and for a true worm's view of a skyscraper. Moderate look-up is a portrait with rank.
Extreme look-up is Worm's-Eye View .
how: Drop the camera below the subject's eyes (chest, waist, or a hole in the floor) and tilt up until verticals converge toward the top of the frame. A wider lens exaggerates the convergence; a longer lens from the same height still looks up but with less stretch.
Practicals on the ceiling become motivated keys. Keep roll level unless you are also doing a Dutch Angle .
Prompt: low-angle looking up, converging verticals, ceiling or sky in frame, not camera on the dirt looking straight up.
when: Use it for power, monument, or intimidation: someone who should fill the doorway. Concrete beat: a standing figure shot from a seated listener, ceiling beams closing over the head.
Do not pitch up on every protagonist as a default poster.
vs: Eye Level keeps the sightline horizontal. Worm's-Eye View looks sharply up from ground or below until the subject is a tower and verticals collapse inward.
Ground Level is a floor-height camera; it may look along the dirt instead of up. High Angle is the opposing pitch.
Trunk Shot looks up from inside a container, which is a location, not only a tilt.
examples_film: Citizen Kane puts ceilings and looming bodies into confrontations by looking up from a lowered camera. Touch of Evil uses the same grammar on Quinlan so bulk becomes the image.
The Dark Knight often pitches up on costume and architecture so the figure reads as a structure. Tokyo Story and Late Spring are the usual mix-up: low seated cameras, mostly level, not this tilt.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Worm's-Eye View or a generic Ground Level boot shot. Tell: only nostrils and a vanishing point in the sky, or only shoes.
Fix: below eye height, tilted up, eyes and mouth still readable, ceiling in. The other mix-up is Ozu: low height, level camera.
If doorways and floor lines stay orthogonal, you never pitched up.

faq.q: What is a low angle in film?
faq.a: A low-angle shot looks up at the subject from below eye level. Verticals converge, ceilings or sky gain area, and the figure reads larger than an eye-level portrait.

faq.q: Low angle vs worm's-eye view
faq.a: A low angle is a moderate look-up that still functions as a face. A worm's-eye view is extreme: lens at or below ground, looking sharply up, verticals collapsing inward, the subject as a tower.

faq.q: When should I use a low angle?
faq.a: Use it when power, monument, or intimidation should be in the geometry: a standing threat over a seated listener, a figure in a doorway. Do not use it as default flattery.

faq.q: How do I prompt a low angle for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Low-angle shot looking up at [Subject], camera below their eyes, converging verticals, ceiling in frame. Say it is not a worm's-eye or floor-only boot shot.

title: Object POV
narrative: Agency leaves the invisible observer and goes to a machine or a thing. A fork of a bicycle stays in the corner while cobbles rush.
A car body is fixed and the desert tears past. A phone slides across a table toward a face.
Sports broadcasts have lived here for decades (puck, stump, helmet). The motion is tactile because the mount cannot independently decide to drift.
It is not First-Person , which is a human body with hands and breath. It is not a free drone that happens to start near a prop.
If the anchor object wanders inside the frame, the parent is broken.
how: Use a professionally secured mount or a rigid virtual parent transform on the named object. Include a visible part of the anchor (barrel, rubber, chrome, glass edge).
Preserve vibration that belongs to the object; do not add a second operator path. Lens choice is often wide because the mount is close.
Prompt: object POV as if [Subject] were seen from a tool, a ball, a bullet, a phone: the thing looking.
when: Use it when the prop has eyes: a weapon, a vehicle, a thrown thing, a camera that is diegetic. Concrete beat: viewpoint from a phone sliding toward a face, the phone's bezel fixed at the frame edge.
Do not use it as a pretty fly-around that ignores the object.
vs: First-Person is a human body owning the lens. Point of View is a character's optical insert, usually without a gadget rim.
Locked-On glues a subject in frame while the world streams; object-POV is looking from the object, often with the object as foreground. Trunk Shot is a pit people open, not a tool in flight.
FPV Drone is a flying body of its own.
examples_film: Mad Max: Fury Road keeps parts of pursuing machines fixed while the desert tears past. Leviathan (2012) mounts cameras on fishing equipment and bodies at sea so the work, not an observer, sees.
Sports broadcasts use puck and vehicle mounts as the same grammar. Hardcore Henry inserts gadget viewpoints inside an otherwise human first-person film.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is First-Person (human hands) or a free-flying camera. Tell: breath and fingers, or the phone drifting around inside the shot.
Fix: parent the camera to the named prop, show the prop's edge, keep that edge locked. If people open a lid and look in, you wanted Trunk Shot .

faq.q: What is object POV in film?
faq.a: Object POV is the viewpoint of a prop or vehicle. The camera is attached to that thing, so the thing stays put in the frame while the world moves.

faq.q: Object POV vs first-person
faq.a: First-person is a human body: hands, breath, eye height of a person. Object POV is a tool, ball, bullet, phone, or machine looking, with the object as the mount.

faq.q: When should I use object POV?
faq.a: Use it when a prop should see: a vehicle chase from the machine, a thrown camera, a diegetic gadget. Do not use it for a person's glance; that is POV or first-person.

faq.q: How do I prompt object POV for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Object POV from [named prop], a piece of the object locked in the foreground, [Subject] seen from that mount, world moving around a rigid camera. For video, the object travels; the camera does not detach.

title: Overhead Top-Down
narrative: This is the crime scene, the place setting, the dance formation, the town drawn as a floor plan. People become pieces in a system.
Shadows draw on the surface because the camera is the ceiling. It can make an ordinary ritual strange by removing the social face.
A steep High Angle still has walls in perspective. A Bird's-Eye View still has altitude and drop.
Overhead wants the tabletop's geometry to match a plan: rectangles stay rectangles. If you still need the eyes, you are in the wrong viewpoint.
how: Mount the camera on an overhead rig, a high grid, or a virtual parent looking down the world Z-axis. Pitch at 90 degrees, roll chosen so the set's long axis sits square.
Arrange performers for silhouette: heads, hands, plates, chalk outlines. Because faces are less available, costume color and contrast have to carry identity.
Prompt: overhead top-down at 90 degrees, flat-lay or room plan, shadows as drawing.
when: Use it for a table, a crime scene, or a dance formation that should read as a diagram. Concrete beat: four pairs of hands setting a long table, plates passing, the rectangle of the wood filling the frame.
Do not use it when the line is on a face.
vs: Bird's-Eye View is a steep look from a great height; overhead is the 90-degree plan, often closer. High Angle is oblique and keeps a readable face.
Crane Over is the move that can finish as this viewpoint. A product flat-lay is the still-life cousin; film overhead usually still includes a body as a piece in the plan.
examples_film: Dogville exposes the town as a floor-plan layout from above. The Grand Budapest Hotel uses top-down desks, pastries, and objects as graphic systems.
Oldboy 's corridor coverage from above turns bodies into a moving diagram. Borrow the plan view, not the wallpaper.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a steep High Angle that still shows a wall and a face. Tell: trapezoid table, eyeline into camera, room in perspective.
Fix: 90 degrees, plan geometry, silhouette clarity. The other failure is a bird's-eye city when you asked for a kitchen table: wrong scale.
Name the surface (table, bed, street as plan) and the distance.

faq.q: What is overhead top-down in film?
faq.a: An overhead shot looks nearly straight down at 90 degrees. Bodies and rooms flatten into a graphic plan; faces give way to silhouette and arrangement.

faq.q: Overhead vs bird's-eye view
faq.a: Overhead is a straight-down plan, often over a table, a body, or a marked floor. Bird's-eye view is from a great height, a map of a place with a sense of drop.

faq.q: When should I use overhead top-down?
faq.a: Use it when systems, evidence, or choreography should be legible as a diagram. Do not use it for a talking face.

faq.q: How do I prompt overhead for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Overhead top-down shot of [Subject] at 90 degrees, flat-lay or room plan, table or floor as a rectangle, shadows as drawing. Forbid an oblique high angle.

title: Point of View
narrative: Classical coverage builds a POV as a sentence: a person looks, we cut to the seen, we often cut back to a reaction. Rear Window lives on that grammar.
The camera sits at their eyes, aims where they aim, and refuses the back of their head. Identification is forced because the audience is briefly the character.

It is not Over-the-Shoulder Coverage , which keeps the looker's shoulder as a claim of with, not as. It is not First-Person , which lets a body own the lens for a long ride: hands, breath, locomotion.
A POV can be a single still insert. First-person is a body that keeps seeing.
Subjective sound (a ringing ear, a mute beach) can ride with a POV or sit on an objective picture. Do not confuse a hearing filter with this optical setup.
how: Put the camera at the named character's eye height and point it along their eyeline. Match lens choice to their attention: a longer glass for binocular looking, a wider field for a panicked scan.
No owner body in frame unless a diegetic visor or mask is the optical device ( Halloween ). If you include a shoulder, you have left POV for OTS.
Prompt: what [Subject] sees, world at their eye height, no back of a head, no shoulder of the looker.
when: Use it to force identification: the audience is the character for the length of the look. Concrete beat: a look offscreen, then empty tracks, steam, and lamps at their eye height.
Do not use it when you still need the looker's face in the same shot; shoot the look, then the POV, or use OTS.
vs: Over-the-Shoulder Coverage shows the near shoulder and the far face; we stand with the looker. First-Person adds hands, breath, and a body that owns the lens over time.
Object POV is a tool or vehicle seeing, not a person. Fourth Wall is the opposite look: eyes into our lens.
SnorriCam straps the camera to the body and looks at their face.
examples_film: Rear Window cuts from Jeff to binocular-aligned views of the courtyard. Halloween 's opening adopts the observer's optical viewpoint through the mask.
Gravity moves into helmet-level seeing. Saving Private Ryan pairs optical shock with Miller's muted hearing; the sound is a cousin, not the definition of the shot.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Over-the-Shoulder Coverage or a face looking toward camera. Tell: a blurry shoulder, the back of a head, or the looker staring at us.
Fix: empty of the owner, eyeline into the scene, height matched to the character you just showed looking. If hands and a gun enter and stay, you drifted into First-Person .

faq.q: What is a POV shot in film?
faq.a: A POV shot shows what a character sees from their eye height. The camera stands in for their eyes; the looker's head and shoulder are not in frame.

faq.q: POV vs over-the-shoulder
faq.a: POV is as the character: no owner body, only the seen world. Over-the-shoulder keeps a near shoulder in the foreground and the far face sharp; we are with them, not inside the look.

faq.q: When should I use a POV shot?
faq.a: Use it after a look, when identification with what they see is the beat: a courtyard, a threat, a visor. Do not use it as the only coverage of a conversation.

faq.q: How do I prompt a POV shot for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: What [Subject] sees at their eye height, no back of head, no looker shoulder, [object of the look] filling the frame. Name whose viewpoint.

title: Profile
narrative: Turn the skull until the far eye disappears. What remains is silhouette, secrecy, and a sightline that refuses us.
A statue, a cameo, a don who will not grant the lens his other eye: profile withholds. The nose becomes a line against the background; the mouth can hide.
It is the wrong tool for most talk. Both eyes are how we read a lie.
If the beat needs charm, pain, or a clear listen, use Three-Quarter Angle . If they look into the lens, you wanted Fourth Wall , not a side.
how: Orbit until the camera sits on a line perpendicular to the subject's median plane. Keep height at Eye Level unless you are adding rank on purpose.
Light can graze the profile so the nose and brow separate from the field, or it can swallow the face into silhouette. Leave look-space in the direction of the nose.
Prompt: true profile, camera at 90 degrees to the head, one ear, nose as architecture, looking offscreen.
when: Use it for statue, secrecy, or a nose as architecture. Concrete beat: a seated power figure in side view, looking toward an offscreen petitioner, one ear and a cigar.
Do not use it as default coverage of a two-person argument; you will lose the eyes.
vs: Three-Quarter Angle turns the face about 45 degrees so both eyes stay visible and the cheek recedes. Eye Level is a height, not a facing; a profile is often eye-level and 90 degrees yaw.
Point of View is the view they see, not the side of their head. Fourth Wall aims the eyes at us, the opposite of an offscreen profile look.
examples_film: Barry Lyndon uses painterly side views so court faces sit like plates without becoming cartoons. The Godfather often parks Vito in profile at the desk, looking toward petitioners rather than toward us.
Borrow the 90-degree head, the offscreen look, and a human face, not a cut-out.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Three-Quarter Angle : both eyes sneak back in. Tell: far iris visible, cheek still facing us.
Fix: rotate until the far eye is gone and the nose breaks the cheek line. The other failure is a paper cut-out with no skull volume.
Ask for a living head, skin, and one ear.

faq.q: What is a profile shot in film?
faq.a: A profile places the camera at 90 degrees to the head. You get one ear, the nose in side view, and a look offscreen; the far eye is hidden.

faq.q: Profile vs three-quarter angle
faq.a: Profile is a true side: one ear, far eye gone. Three-quarter turns the face about 45 degrees so both eyes remain and the far cheek recedes.

faq.q: When should I use a profile shot?
faq.a: Use it for concealment, formality, or a sightline that belongs offscreen. Do not use it when you need both eyes to carry a line.

faq.q: How do I prompt a profile for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: True profile of [Subject], camera at 90 degrees to the head, one ear, nose as architecture, looking offscreen, far eye hidden. Say a human face, not a stamped portrait.

title: Reverse Angle
narrative: Someone looks. The reverse is who or what occupies the other pole.
In a diner, it is the other booth. In a gunfight, it is the other holster.
Matching size and height keeps the cut from feeling like a new scene. The reverse can be a clean Single or an Over-the-Shoulder Coverage ; the name is the axis, not the foreground shoulder.
Withholding the reverse is a different editorial choice: a look, a reaction, and no answering view. The Blair Witch Project and Rosemary's Baby live on that denial.
The reverse-angle shot itself is the answering camera, not the refusal of it.
