how: Hold the 180-line. Move the camera to the opposite side of the axis, still on the same side of the line, and match lens height to the new subject (sit versus stand, adult versus child).
Match shot size to the outgoing picture unless the cut is meant to punch. Eyelines must cross the same empty air.
Prompt: reverse angle, opposing view of the dialogue or standoff, 180-line respected, geography flipping.
when: Use it to complete the axis: show who they were looking at. Concrete beat: after a look across a table, the matching-size single of the other person, eyeline opposing.
Do not fire the reverse when the scene's power is the withheld object of the look.
vs: Over-the-Shoulder Coverage is a composition often used as the reverse, with a near shoulder; a reverse can also be a clean Single . Point of View shows what they see, which may not be a face.
Eye Level may match on both sides, but the reverse is the opposing camera, not a height. Profile two-shots can reverse into opposing profiles.
examples_film: Heat 's diner keeps clear opposing screen directions on two three-quarter singles. The Good, the Bad and the Ugly builds the cemetery standoff from answering views along one axis.
The Shining 's red-bathroom talk uses startling opposing spatial views. Neighbors (1920) is an early lesson in preserving orientation across reverses.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a new setup that crosses the line or changes size for no reason. Tell: both faces look camera-right, or a wide answering a choker.
Fix: opposing eyelines, matched height and size, 180-line held. The other mix-up is Point of View : an empty doorway they were watching is a POV, not a reverse on the other person.

faq.q: What is a reverse angle in film?
faq.a: A reverse angle shows the same spatial relationship from the opposing side. It completes a look or a dialogue axis while keeping the 180-degree line.

faq.q: Reverse angle vs over-the-shoulder
faq.a: A reverse is the opposing camera on the axis. Over-the-shoulder is a framing that often serves as that reverse, with a near shoulder in the foreground. The reverse can also be a clean single.

faq.q: When should I use a reverse angle?
faq.a: Use it when the audience must see the other pole of a look, a talk, or a standoff. Do not use it when withholding the object of the look is the point.

faq.q: How do I prompt a reverse angle for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Reverse angle on [Subject], opposing view of the dialogue or standoff, 180-line respected, matching size, eyeline opposite the first shot. Name the geography that should flip.

title: Shoulder Level
narrative: You stay with a mover without dropping into chaotic Handheld grammar. The lens is where another body would be: beside them on a street, a few inches low, able to take a bump.
Hurt Locker bomb walks and Goodfellas nightclub approaches often live in this band because the camera can travel as a person would. It is not Over-the-Shoulder Coverage .
OTS is a foreground shoulder of a different body. Shoulder-level can be a clean Single or a Follow Shot with no near shoulder at all.
The name is pedestal height.
how: Set the camera at clavicle or deltoid height, typically 5 to 20 cm below the subject's eyes. Keep the horizon close to level; a tiny look-up is natural from this height and should not grow into a power tilt.
A 35mm is a common walking companion. Stabilization ( Steadicam , Gimbal Shot ) keeps the height without adding shake as style.
Prompt: shoulder-level camera, slightly below the eyes, walking companion's view.
when: Use it to stay with a mover as a companion, especially through rooms and streets. Concrete beat: walking a few feet off a soldier or a host, lens at their shoulder, face readable, floor not dominating.
Do not use it as a substitute for messy handheld, and do not call an OTS this unless the only fact you mean is height.
vs: Eye Level matches the pupils and reads as equal portrait. Hip Level drops to the belt.
Low Angle pitches up on purpose. Over-the-Shoulder Coverage includes a near person's shoulder; shoulder-level need not.
Point of View removes the companion and becomes the mover's eyes. Follow Shot is the path; shoulder-level is the height of that path.
examples_film: The Hurt Locker often stays at soldier height through streets and rooms so the walk is shared, not observed from a balcony. Goodfellas ' Copacabana approach rides at companion height through the kitchen: we arrive with Henry, not as his eyes and not as a crane.
Borrow the pedestal, not the whole tracking route.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is true Eye Level (too high and formal) or a Low Angle (too much pitch). Tell: matched pupils, or a ceiling grab.
Fix: camera at the shoulder, slight look-up at most, companion distance. If a blurry shoulder of another actor eats the frame, you wrote OTS.
If hands of the subject enter as if we were them, you wrote First-Person .

faq.q: What is shoulder level in film?
faq.a: Shoulder-level places the camera slightly below the subject's eyes, at walking-companion height. It is a pedestal choice, usually with a nearly level horizon.

faq.q: Shoulder level vs eye level
faq.a: Eye level matches the pupils and reads as equal, formal coverage. Shoulder level sits a few inches lower, like a person walking beside them, less of a portrait lock.

faq.q: When should I use shoulder level?
faq.a: Use it to stay with a mover without a power tilt or a formal eye lock. Do not use it when you need peer-to-peer stillness or a holster-plane standoff.

faq.q: How do I prompt shoulder level for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Shoulder-level camera on [Subject], slightly below the eyes, walking companion's view, horizon nearly level. Say not eye-level and not a low-angle. For motion, follow at that height.

title: Three-Quarter Angle
narrative: Most coverage of a talking face lives here. You see both eyes, the bridge of the nose, and a cheek going away, which is enough skull to light and enough access to read a listen.

It is useful because it models the head and still connects to an offscreen partner along a natural eyeline. It is the wrong tool when you want a coin (use Profile ) or a confession into the taking lens (use Fourth Wall ).
It is also not a height: you can shoot three-quarter from Eye Level , Low Angle , or High Angle . The name is yaw, not tilt.
how: Place the camera about 30 to 50 degrees off the subject's nose. Keep both irises; hide only a sliver of the far ear if any.
A 50mm to 85mm holds the head without stretching the near eye. Key from the far or near side depending on short or broad lighting; the angle is what gives the planes.
Prompt: three-quarter angle, face turned about 45 degrees, both eyes, classic portrait dimensionality.
when: Use it as the default narrative portrait when a face must have volume and still belong to a scene. Concrete beat: a diner single, body open 45 degrees, eyeline to the partner off left, both eyes sharp.
Do not use it when concealment is the point; rotate to Profile .
vs: Profile is 90 degrees, one ear, far eye gone. Eye Level is how high the camera sits; three-quarter is how the head is turned.
Over-the-Shoulder Coverage often holds a three-quarter far face with a near shoulder chewing the frame. A full-front look into lens is Fourth Wall or an Interview eyeline, not three-quarter.
examples_film: Heat 's diner encounter parks two faces in three-quarter so each man remains a full head while screen direction stays clean. Classical portrait coverage from studio-era close-ups through drawing-room films uses the same 45-degree turn to model a cheek.
Borrow the yaw and the two eyes, not a copied booth.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Profile (too much turn) or a passport front (too little). Tell: far eye gone, or both ears equally seen.
Fix: about 45 degrees, both irises, one ear dominant. The other failure is calling a Low Angle a three-quarter.
Pitch is not yaw; say both.

faq.q: What is a three-quarter angle in film?
faq.a: A three-quarter angle turns the face about 45 degrees to camera. Both eyes stay visible and the far cheek recedes, which is the default narrative portrait.

faq.q: Three-quarter angle vs profile
faq.a: Three-quarter keeps both eyes and a receding cheek. Profile is a 90-degree side view: one ear, nose as a line, far eye hidden.

faq.q: When should I use a three-quarter angle?
faq.a: Use it for most talking portraits that still need a connection to an offscreen partner. Use profile to withhold, or a look into lens to admit the audience.

faq.q: How do I prompt a three-quarter angle for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Three-quarter angle on [Subject], face turned about 45 degrees, both eyes visible, far cheek receding. Name camera height separately. Not profile, not into the lens.

title: Trunk Shot
narrative: The audience is the object or the concealed body. Two faces appear over a bright lid; they look down at us; the dark rim eats the edges.

Power and curiosity swap: the standing people have the height, the camera has the secret. Tarantino's crime grammar made the car trunk a signature, but any container (a crate, an instrument case) can host the same physics.
A Low Angle on a street has no lid. A Worm's-Eye View on a tower has no one looking into the lens.
If you cannot see the opening, you do not have the shot.
how: Put a low camera in a trunk, a box, or an open-bottom set piece. Keep the container edge in frame on several sides.
Stage the lid's movement and aim the actors' eyelines at the same interior point. Daylight or a parking-lamp key from above is motivated by the open lid; the interior stays in shadow.
Prompt: trunk shot looking up from inside a car trunk or confined pit, rim framing the faces.
when: Use it when someone is in the trunk, or when the reveal should come from inside a container. Concrete beat: two people pop a lid and lean in, looking down at the lens, dark rim against a bright sky.
Do not use it as a decorative low-angle on standing gangsters with no car.
vs: Low Angle looks up without a container. Worm's-Eye View looks up at architecture from the dirt.

Object POV can live inside a thing, but usually as the thing moving through the world, not as people opening it. Point of View of a bound captive can coincide with a trunk shot when the occupant is a character we have already met.
examples_film: Pulp Fiction views Jules and Vincent from inside the car trunk as they look down. Reservoir Dogs stages the same downward look into an open trunk.
Kill Bill and From Dusk Till Dawn reuse the pit-and-lid grammar. Borrow the rim, the lid, and the eyelines into the box.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a generic Low Angle in a driveway. Tell: full standing bodies, no lid, no rim, horizon of a parking lot.
Fix: inside the trunk, rim in frame, faces leaning over an opening, downward eyelines. If the camera floats up and reveals the observer, you left the container.

faq.q: What is a trunk shot in film?
faq.a: A trunk shot looks up from inside a car trunk or similar pit. The lid and rim frame people looking down, so the camera sits where an object or captive would sit.

faq.q: Trunk shot vs low angle
faq.a: A low angle looks up from below eye level anywhere. A trunk shot is specifically inside a container; without the opening and the rim, it is just a low angle.

faq.q: When should I use a trunk shot?
faq.a: Use it when the viewpoint belongs in a trunk, a crate, or a case, and the standing people are looking in. Do not use it as a style sticker on any crime scene.

faq.q: How do I prompt a trunk shot for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Trunk shot looking up at [Subject] from inside a car trunk, dark rim framing the faces, lid open, actors looking down into the lens. Say the camera stays in the pit.

title: Worm's-Eye View
narrative: This is not a slightly taller portrait. The lens is on or under the floor plane and the look is nearly straight up: nostrils, cornices, the belly of a ship, a ceiling that has become the whole sky.
Wonder and terror share the same geometry because scale has nowhere to go but over you. Use a Low Angle when you still need a face that can speak.
Use Ground Level when the dirt, the boots, and the trailing hem are the actors and the look may travel along the ground rather than up the body. Worm's-eye is the vanishing point in the zenith.
how: Put the lens on the floor, in a pit, or at ground grade. Tilt up hard, often past 60 degrees, until architecture converges to a point above the frame.
Ultra-wide glass increases the collapse; keep anatomy plausible (one head, two feet). Foreground may include earth, a curb, or a grating.

faq.a: Choreo is a camera that shares a count with the bodies: one phrase of movement, then a stop, as if the lens were a dance partner.

faq.q: Choreo vs Steadicam
faq.a: Steadicam is a stabilizer. Choreo is the idea that blocking and lens are timed together; it can ride a vest, a dolly, or a jib.

faq.q: When should I use Choreo?
faq.a: Use it for a dance, a fight, or a walk written as one musical sentence. Do not use it as default coverage.

faq.q: How do I prompt Choreo for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write bodies and lens on one phrase, then stop. Example: Choreographed camera with [Subject], bodies and lens timed together, one phrase of movement, dance-floor blocking.

title: Conveyor
narrative: Industry, process, no escape from the line. The shot says labor is a machine: bodies, boxes, or faces arrive and leave at one speed.
Comedy and paranoia both live here. It is the wrong tool for a walker you are meant to accompany.
If the person is choosing a path, truck or track with them. A conveyor that speeds up and slows with emotion is no longer a belt.
how: Lateral dolly, slider, or a treadmill-like set, constant velocity, often a wide or moderate-wide so units repeat. Foreground machinery should cross faster than the far wall.

Exposure can be industrial: hard practicals, green or sodium, no beauty key. Prompt: Conveyor move past [Subject], the world sliding on a belt, factory or infinite product line, relentless lateral travel.
when: Use it for a factory, an assembly of faces, a process that will not stop. Do not use it beside a casual sidewalk chat.
vs: Trucking stays beside a walker; speed is human. Tracking Shot follows a chosen path.
Conveyor is the line that does not care. A Dolly can go any direction; this one is lateral and metronomic.
examples_film: Modern Times turns the factory into a belt the body cannot leave. The Parallax View uses industrial process and test-film geometry as a trap.
Grammar: constant lateral speed, repeating units.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a trucking shot with a walker. The tell: the subject is strolling and the camera is being polite.
The fix: constant lateral speed, repeating units, the person as another item on the line.

faq.q: What is Conveyor in film?
faq.a: A conveyor camera is relentless lateral travel at constant speed, as if the world were a factory belt. The subject can be still while units keep arriving.

faq.q: Conveyor vs Trucking
faq.a: Trucking stays beside a person walking. Conveyor is industrial: one speed, repeating units, process without escape.

faq.q: When should I use Conveyor?
faq.a: Use it for factories, process, and systems that swallow people. Do not use it for a casual walk-and-talk.

faq.q: How do I prompt Conveyor for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write constant lateral speed and a belt or product line. Example: Conveyor move past [Subject], the world sliding on a belt, factory or infinite product line, relentless lateral travel.

title: Crane Down
narrative: Arrive from a god-view into a person without resetting attention. What begins as an overview can become an intimate encounter in one path.

Some famous descents even hand off from crane to ground support and keep walking. It is the wrong tool when you only need to look down from a locked roof, or when a cut from aerial to close-up would be cleaner.
Do not assume every continuous-looking descent was achieved without a join.
how: Plan the high composition and the human landing. The arm descends, often moving forward as well, with a remote head keeping the subject framed.
If you add a support handoff, match direction, speed, height, and horizon at the transfer. Prompt a crane down from a high wide view into a closer frame, map collapsing to face.
when: Use it to arrive from god-view into a person. Concrete beat: a valley of tents, then one volunteer with a bag.
Do not tour on the way down.
vs: A Crane Up leaves the person for the map. A Tilt Down only pitches from one height.
A Pedestal Down drops on a column with tilt locked and little or no boom. An Aerial Push In starts higher still, from helicopter or drone altitude.
examples_film: Bound for Glory descends from a crane in the migrant camp and continues at ground level. Contact 's VLA shot descends and continues with Ellie toward a building.
I Am Cuba traverses spaces with extraordinary continuous-looking movement. The Shining and Magnolia also use descending arms as arrival.
Check each shot's joins before claiming a single rig.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Tilt Down or a cut from aerial to close-up. The tell is a nodding camera that never loses altitude, or a scale jump.
The fix: continuous descent of the station point, matched horizon, a readable human landing.

faq.q: What is Crane Down in film?
faq.a: It is a physical descent of the camera on a crane or jib from a high view into a closer, human-scale composition.

faq.q: Crane Down vs Tilt Down
faq.a: Tilt down looks down from a fixed height. Crane down moves the camera through height, so you actually arrive at the person.

faq.q: When should I use Crane Down?
faq.a: When an overview should become an encounter without a cut. Do not use it if you only needed to glance at the floor.

faq.q: How do I prompt Crane Down for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write crane down from a high wide view into a closer frame on [Subject], continuous descent, no cut to aerial. Name the landing size.

title: Crane Over
narrative: The shot turns a scene into a diagram without cutting. Bodies, tables, and streets become plan view because the arm has climbed and pitched over them.
It is not a still overhead: the audience rides the change of rank. It is the wrong tool when you already want a locked top-down, or when a simple crane-up should keep looking forward at a skyline.
If you never reach a downward angle, you only craned up.
how: Boom up and arc forward, remote head tilting down as the arm passes over the subject. End nearly nadir or at a steep high angle.
Watch for the subject being covered by the arm's shadow and for changing key as you face new windows. Prompt a crane over, arm rising and arcing forward until the camera looks nearly straight down.
when: Use it to turn a scene into a map without cutting. Concrete beat: a dinner argument, then the table as a chessboard.
Do not crane over if the last frame is still a forward wide.
vs: A Crane Up typically keeps a forward look as it rises and eases back. An Overhead Top-Down can be a locked top-down with no ride.
A Jib Shot can do a small version of this arc over a table. Crane over is the continuous climb into downward view.
examples_film: The Untouchables uses crane height over the Union Station staircase so the action becomes a diagram of steps and bodies. Birdman rides theater space until floor plans and faces share one path.
Use the arc-into-down, not the period costumes.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Crane Up that never looks down, or a cut to Overhead Top-Down . The tell is a forward skyline at the end, or a jump to top-down.
The fix: one arm path that finishes steeply downward, subject still readable as a map.

faq.q: What is Crane Over in film?
faq.a: It is a crane move that rises and arcs until the camera looks down, combining a height change with a change of angle in one path.

faq.q: Crane Over vs Crane Up
faq.a: Crane up usually eases back while still looking across the world. Crane over continues until the view is downward and the floor becomes the picture.

faq.q: When should I use Crane Over?
faq.a: When blocking should become a map without a cut. Do not use it if you wanted a skyline or a still overhead lock-off.

faq.q: How do I prompt Crane Over for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write crane up and over [Subject], finishing nearly straight down. One continuous arm move. Ban a cut to top-down.

title: Crane Over The Head
narrative: Finish by looking down. A body on a floor, a crime, a dance, a figure lost in pattern: the arm climbs and continues until the lens is almost nadir.
A crane-up that eases back into a skyline is a different end: the person becomes geography from an oblique height. Overhead and bird's-eye can be locked.
This shot is the travel that arrives there.
how: Jib or Technocrane, start at human height or a three-quarter, boom up and over until tilt is nearly 90 degrees down. A little boom-out keeps the subject from sliding off.
Prompt: Crane over the head of [Subject], the arm rising until the camera looks nearly straight down, a person becoming a map.
when: Use it to end on a downward map of a person. Do not stop at a high three-quarter and call it over the head.
vs: Crane Over travels the arm over an obstacle or crowd without requiring nadir. Overhead Top-Down is the locked top-down frame.
Bird's-Eye View is the high downward view as a size. Crane-over-the-head is the boom that becomes those views.
examples_film: The Untouchables uses high downward cranes (the station, the pram, the floor as a map). Birdman booms over theater space until people become pattern.
Grammar: rise until you look down.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a crane-up that stays oblique, or a locked overhead with no travel. The tell: we never look down, or we were already down.
The fix: boom up and over until the lens is nearly straight down.

faq.q: What is Crane Over The Head in film?
faq.a: A crane over the head booms up and over a person until the camera looks nearly straight down. The person becomes a map.

faq.q: Crane Over The Head vs Overhead Top-Down
faq.a: Overhead is the locked top-down frame. Crane over the head is the travel that arrives there from a human starting height.

faq.q: When should I use Crane Over The Head?
faq.a: Use it to finish by looking down on a person. Do not stop at a high three-quarter.

faq.q: How do I prompt Crane Over The Head for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write a boom that ends almost straight down. Example: Crane over the head of [Subject], the arm rising until the camera looks nearly straight down, a person becoming a map.

title: Crane Up
narrative: A crane-up starts at human height and leaves it. The person stays in frame, then the rooftops, then the city.
By the end, the figure is one dark coat in a much larger night. Use it when the scene needs to end, or when a private moment has to admit the world that contains it.
A tilt up only changes the angle. A crane changes the map.
Do not use it as decoration on every wide. If nothing new appears as the camera climbs, the move is empty.
how: The operator rides or remote-heads a crane. The arm can be a few feet (a jib) or tens of feet (a Technocrane).

Keep a foreground anchor visible during the rise so the newly revealed scale has a reference. Prompt crane up and slightly back, name the start (shoulder height, waist, close-up), and name the reveal (rooftops, canyon, overpass).
If you only write camera goes up, you often get a tilt or a cheap zoom.
when: Use it to end a scene, reveal a city, or turn a person into landscape. Concrete beat: a woman on a wet roof, then the square below takes the frame.
Do not crane up if the last frame shows nothing the first frame did not already imply.
vs: A Tilt Up rotates on a fixed tripod. A Jib Shot is the short-arm version of this family.
An Aerial Pullback continues until geography wins completely from helicopter or high-drone height. A Pull Out stays at eye height and only retreats.
Crane Down arrives at a face instead of leaving one.
examples_film: The opening of Touch of Evil treats the crane as a long sentence through a border town. The wounded-field pullaway in Gone with the Wind turns a person into a statistic of war.
La La Land lets hillside and dock cranes sit romance in a real city. The Player opens on studio-lot crane choreography.
Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Tilt Up or a cut from close-up to aerial. The tell is no parallax, or a jump in scale with no continuous ascent.
The fix: physical rise plus a little boom-out, a visible foreground anchor, continuity of the figure all the way up.

faq.q: What is Crane Up in film?
faq.a: It is a physical lift of the camera on a jib or crane, often easing back, so a human-scale frame becomes a wider view of the place.

faq.q: Crane Up vs Tilt Up
faq.a: A tilt rotates the camera on a fixed tripod. A crane physically moves the camera through space, so foreground, mid-ground, and background change in parallax.

faq.q: When should I use Crane Up?
faq.a: When a scene should close, or a private beat must admit the city, crowd, or land that contains it. Do not use it if the climb reveals nothing new.

faq.q: How do I prompt Crane Up for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name starting height, crane up and slightly back, and what is revealed. Example: camera cranes up and slightly back from shoulder height, revealing rooftops and the city beyond.

title: Crash Zoom In
narrative: The shot punctuates a hit, a name, a weapon, or a comic sting. Artificiality is the point.
The audience is not invited to approach; they are struck by a lens. It is the wrong tool for a thought that should land over several seconds, and the wrong tool for geography.
After the snap, hold. If you keep zooming or add shake, the sting becomes noise.
how: Keep the subject on the zoom center. Use a controlled fast zoom or, in post, a high-resolution crop that still behaves like optics, not a warp.
Expect radial motion blur during the snap, then a hard hold on the tight frame. Avoid autofocus hunting.
Prompt an aggressive optical punch-in under one second, zoom blur, then a locked tight hold, and ban a physical dolly.
when: Use it to punctuate a hit, a realization, or a comic sting. Concrete beat: a name is spoken and the face slams into close-up.
Do not use it as a substitute for walking closer through a room.
vs: A Slow Zoom In is the same optical family at patience speed. A Dolly In has parallax and feels like a person stepping in.
A Whip Pan blurs by rotating the head, not by changing focal length. Crash zoom in is a snap of the lens, then a hold.
examples_film: Django Unchained uses abrupt zooms as Western punctuation. The Grand Budapest Hotel snaps to comic information.
Kill Bill and Hot Fuzz treat the crash zoom as genre grammar rather than invisibility. Use the speed and the hold, not the costumes.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a fast Dolly In or a Whip Pan . The tell is parallax or horizontal streaking instead of radial zoom blur.
The fix: camera body still, subject on center, snap, then freeze the tight frame. Do not add unrelated camera shake.

faq.q: What is Crash Zoom In in film?
faq.a: It is a very fast increase of focal length that slams from a wider shot into a detail, usually from a locked camera, then holds.

faq.q: Crash Zoom In vs Dolly In
faq.a: Dolly in moves the camera through space. Crash zoom in changes only the lens, often with radial blur, and reads as a punctuation mark rather than an approach.

faq.q: When should I use Crash Zoom In?
faq.a: When a fact must hit: a face, a gun, a title, a joke. Use it once per beat and hold. Do not use it to tour a location.

faq.q: How do I prompt Crash Zoom In for AI image or video?
faq.a: Demand a snap optical zoom in under one second, radial zoom blur, a still camera body, and a hard hold. Ban dolly and extra shake.

title: Crash Zoom Out
narrative: Scale, danger, or a joke appears all at once. The close moment is undercut because the world was always that large; the lens simply confessed.
The snap is the comedy or the horror, not a polite reveal. It is the wrong tool when you need to walk backward through furniture, or when the newly revealed space must pass the camera in layers.
Optical dump is not a retreat.
how: Lock the body. Center the zoom so the subject does not smear sideways.
Snap from the tight composition to a pre-composed wide in under a second, then hold the wide. Radial blur during the change, not handheld bounce.
Prompt a sudden crash zoom out, environment exploding into view, then a locked wide hold.
when: Use it to shock-reveal scale or undercut a close moment. Concrete beat: an intimate two-shot snaps to a parking lot full of witnesses.
Do not use it when the camera must physically leave the subject.
vs: A Crash Zoom In punches the other way, into a detail. A Pull Out translates the camera backward with parallax.
A Slow Zoom Out discloses the same optical widening without the sting. Crash zoom out is the dump, then the hold.
examples_film: Shaun of the Dead snaps from faces into wider comic geography. Evil Dead uses violent optical widening as shock.
Hot Fuzz works the same family in both directions. Copy the snap-and-hold, not the gag content.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Dolly Out or a Crash Zoom In fired in the wrong direction. The tell is sliding foreground or a punch that gets tighter instead of wider.
The fix: locked body, pre-composed wide end, snap out, hold.

faq.q: What is Crash Zoom Out in film?
faq.a: It is a very fast decrease of focal length that throws a tight image into a wide one, usually from a still camera, then holds the wide.

faq.q: Crash Zoom Out vs Pull Out
faq.a: A pull out moves the camera away so space opens with parallax. A crash zoom out only widens the lens, so the station point never changes.

faq.q: When should I use Crash Zoom Out?
faq.a: When you need an instant scale joke, a threat revealed around a close face, or a hard undercut. Do not use it as a slow exit.

faq.q: How do I prompt Crash Zoom Out for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write snap zoom out in under a second, camera body still, environment appearing at once, then a locked wide hold. Ban physical retreat.

title: Dolly
narrative: Walk the camera. Change geography.
In, out, or beside: the point is that the support rolls, so space is proven by relative motion. A face can grow because you approached, not because the glass got longer.
A zoom is the wrong cousin when you need the room to be real. If you only need a tighter crop from sticks, zoom.
If the floor cannot take track, say so and use a vest or a crane instead of faking wheels.
how: Lay level track or dance the wheels on a floor. Height is set by the column (often eye or chest).
In and out ride the lens axis; a lateral truck is still a dolly. Keep the horizon honest.
Prompt: Dolly toward or beside [Subject], camera body traveling on a smooth path, true parallax, not a zoom.
when: Use it when the camera must walk: approach a face, leave a room, slide a corridor. Do not call a zoom a dolly.
vs: Dolly In and Dolly Out name the axis along the lens. Tracking Shot follows a moving subject.
A Zoom changes focal length with the body still, so there is no parallax. A Push In is often a vest or a looser approach; a dolly is wheels and a path.
examples_film: The Shining rolls the camera through hotel geometry until space feels like a trap. Goodfellas uses wheeled and vest travel as continuous geography.
Grammar: the body moves, the room shears.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a zoom. The tell: near and far enlarge together, no shear of a lamp or a door frame.
The fix: write physical travel and true parallax, and name the path.

faq.q: What is Dolly in film?
faq.a: A dolly shot is a camera on a wheeled platform that translates through space, producing parallax. It is a physical path, not a zoom.

faq.q: Dolly vs Zoom
faq.a: A zoom changes focal length from a locked body, so space flattens or opens without parallax. A dolly moves the camera, so near objects shear against far ones.

faq.q: When should I use Dolly?
faq.a: Use it when geography must change by walking the camera. Do not use the word dolly for a zoom from sticks.

faq.q: How do I prompt Dolly for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write a traveling camera body and true parallax. Example: Dolly toward or beside [Subject], camera body traveling on a smooth path, true parallax, not a zoom.
